items.title: docs-assistant
items.tagline: An AI support assistant that answers from your documents, cites every answer, and hands the conversation to a person when it doesn't know.
items.description: An embeddable RAG chatbot in .NET 10: hybrid search in PostgreSQL with pgvector, Claude Haiku behind a swappable port, and a 9 KB widget that installs with one line.

metrics.label: retrieval hit@5 on a 54-question bilingual eval

video.caption: 75 seconds on a demo store. On-screen text in Spanish, answers by Claude Haiku 5.5.

caseStudy.context: Small businesses answer the same questions all day, and generic chatbots make up answers that the business then has to correct. The goal was an assistant a customer can trust: it answers only from the business’s own documents, shows where each answer came from, and when it cannot answer, it says so and passes the conversation to a person.
constraints: No invented answers: abstaining beats guessing
Questions and documents in different languages, Spanish and English
A small, visible cost per answer, with hard spending caps
It has to embed in any website without breaking its styles
Several businesses on one deployment, each seeing only its own data
architecture: Documents (PDF, DOCX, Markdown and web pages) are split along their structure and indexed twice in PostgreSQL: as vectors, for meaning across languages, and as full text, for exact words, numbers and names.
A question searches both indexes and the two rankings are fused with Reciprocal Rank Fusion. Passages shaped like injected instructions are quarantined before they reach the model.

Below a measured similarity floor the assistant abstains without calling the model. Otherwise Claude answers from those passages only and cites them as [1], [2]; the citations are validated before the answer streams to the widget over SSE.
The widget is framework-free TypeScript inside a Shadow DOM: 9 KB, one script tag, and styles that never leak into the host page.

decisions.title: Abstain before calling the model
decisions.rationale: When retrieval finds nothing similar enough, the answer is “I can’t find that” plus a person, decided in code at zero cost.
decisions.tradeoff: A few answerable questions are refused when retrieval misses. The eval tracks that rate, so the floor is tuned on data rather than taste.

decisions.title: Hybrid search, not vectors alone
decisions.rationale: Vectors handle meaning and cross-language questions; full text catches the prices, codes and names that embeddings blur. Guaranteeing one vector hit in the fused list raised cross-lingual hit@5 from 86% to 95%.
decisions.tradeoff: Two indexes to maintain and a fusion step to tune, though both live in the PostgreSQL the app already needs.

decisions.title: The model behind a port, with spending guards
decisions.rationale: Claude sits behind Microsoft.Extensions.AI, so the model is a configuration choice, and an extractive mode works with no model at all. The evals refuse to spend without an explicit flag, a call cap and a cost cap.
decisions.tradeoff: A thin abstraction layer to keep current, in exchange for never being locked to one provider or surprised by a bill.

results: Retrieval finds the right passage for 98% of the 54 eval questions, and for 95% when the question and the document are in different languages.
With Claude Haiku 5.5: 0 invalid citations, abstention on 100% of the unanswerable questions, and USD 0.33 per 1,000 questions.
12 of 12 prompt-injection attacks resisted (8 direct, 4 hidden inside documents), while 0 of the 54 real questions were wrongly refused.
Every number comes from an eval in the repository that anyone can rerun, and CI fails if retrieval drops below its thresholds.

items.title: talent-mcp
items.tagline: An MCP server in C# that gives AI agents typed, secured tools for recruiting, built on the session-less 2026-07-28 protocol revision.
items.description: Six typed tools for job search, candidate-fit scoring and skill extraction, over stateless Streamable HTTP with OAuth 2.1 + PKCE, and the same six over stdio as a dotnet tool. Published on NuGet.

metrics.label: typed tools, each behind its own OAuth scope
cold start of the dotnet tool, measured in CI
test levels that gate every merge

caseStudy.context: AI agents are only as useful as the tools they can call safely. The 2026-07-28 revision of the Model Context Protocol removed sessions and server-initiated requests, which breaks the usual ways of paging results and of asking the user for confirmation. talent-mcp is a reference server for that revision, in a domain where mistakes are costly: recruiting.
constraints: No server sessions: any replica must be able to serve any request
Destructive actions need explicit confirmation, without server-initiated requests
Authorization per tool: read, write and destructive scopes are not interchangeable
Reproducible results, so the scoring can serve as a test oracle
architecture: Clean Architecture with the dependency rule enforced by architecture tests in CI. Domain references nothing; Application holds the use cases and ports; Infrastructure holds the EF Core, Keycloak and OpenTelemetry adapters.
The six tools live in one project that two hosts share verbatim: an ASP.NET Core Streamable HTTP server shipped as a container image, and a stdio host shipped as a dotnet tool.

State between calls travels as a signed, time-limited handle passed back as an ordinary tool argument. The client’s trace context arrives in _meta, so a single trace spans client, server and PostgreSQL.

decisions.title: No LLM inside the server
decisions.rationale: Scoring and skill normalization are pure functions, so the server needs no API keys, costs nothing to run and returns the same answer every time.
decisions.tradeoff: Less flexible than asking a model; the agent on the other side brings the language understanding.

decisions.title: Signed handles instead of sessions
decisions.rationale: Pagination state is encoded, signed and time-limited inside the handle itself, so the HTTP host scales horizontally with no sticky sessions and no shared cache.
decisions.tradeoff: Handles are opaque and they expire; a client that holds one too long has to search again.

decisions.title: Tools registered explicitly, not by assembly scan
decisions.rationale: A trimmed build that silently drops its tools answers -32601 with no crash and no error log. Explicit registration, plus a conformance test that asserts all six tools by name, makes that failure loud.
decisions.tradeoff: Adding a tool means touching the registration as well as writing the tool.

results: Published on NuGet as a reusable toolkit library and as the talent-mcp dotnet tool, with a container image on GHCR.
Five test levels gate every merge, from architecture rules to end-to-end runs through OAuth and PostgreSQL.
The Tasks store is verified to survive a database restart, recovering its connections in about a second.
Cold start of the installed dotnet tool measured in CI at 323 ms.

items.title: claude-pr-review-bot
items.tagline: A pull request reviewer for GitHub Actions that asks Claude for one document of findings, and can only ever comment.
items.description: C# on .NET 10. Structured output against a JSON Schema, a single read_file tool, findings filtered against the lines GitHub accepts, and one review per run. It never approves, requests changes or blocks a merge.

metrics.label: estimated per 400-line pull request on Claude Opus 5
tool: read_file, fetched by SHA from the API
permissions to approve, block or merge

caseStudy.context: The obvious AI reviewer gives the model a post-comment tool and executes each call as it arrives. That costs a round trip per finding, can leave half a review behind when a call times out, and never gives the code a moment to see the whole set and decide it is noise. An early version left 47 comments on one pull request, most of them on generated files.
constraints: It must review pull requests from forks, which needs secrets under pull_request_target
Contributor code must never run next to the API key
A prompt injection inside a diff must not be able to approve or block anything
A predictable, visible cost per pull request
architecture: The bot fetches the changed files and their patches from the GitHub API and parses the hunks into the set of lines GitHub will accept a comment on.

Claude receives the diff as untrusted content and returns its findings as one document that conforms to a JSON Schema. When a hunk is a keyhole, it can call read_file, which fetches the file at the head SHA through a path check.
A filter drops findings outside the diff, keeps the most severe one per line and caps the total. Then a single COMMENT review is posted, and every dropped finding is logged.

decisions.title: Findings as data, not actions
decisions.rationale: Structured output returns the whole set at once, so the code can filter, deduplicate and cap it before anything reaches GitHub, and a failure posts nothing instead of half a review.
decisions.tradeoff: The review appears all at once at the end of the run instead of comment by comment.

decisions.title: Comment-only by construction
decisions.rationale: The GitHub client has five methods, and none of them can approve, request changes or merge. The worst a prompt injection can do is make the bot go quiet.
decisions.tradeoff: It cannot enforce anything; a team that wants a blocking gate keeps it in its own CI.

decisions.title: Built from source on every run
decisions.rationale: The composite action compiles the bot at the pinned ref, so the code reviewing your pull request is exactly the code in the repository.
decisions.tradeoff: About a minute per run; a Docker action would be faster but less transparent.

results: About USD 0.12 per 400-line pull request on Claude Opus 5 and about USD 0.05 on Sonnet 5, with input, output and cache-read tokens logged per turn.
A cached system prompt, plus a built-in ignore list for lockfiles and generated code that more than halved the average diff sent to the model.
A dry-run mode with fixture findings exercises the whole pipeline in CI on every push, with no API key.
The design is explained in a DEV.to article, in English and in Spanish.

about.title: About Me
about.subtitle: Get to know me better
about.bio: Senior Software Engineer with 15+ years building and modernizing .NET systems for multinational companies and the public sector. Today I pair that foundation with applied AI: RAG assistants that cite their sources, MCP servers for agents and Claude-powered code review, each measured with quality and cost evals. I work end to end, from architecture and backend to frontend, CI/CD and the cloud, and I lead teams with agile practices.

expertise.ai: RAG assistants on PostgreSQL and pgvector, MCP servers and agents with Claude behind Microsoft.Extensions.AI. Evals in CI, spending guards and prompt-injection defenses.
expertise.frontend: Modern web applications with React, Next.js, TypeScript, and Angular. Expertise in building responsive, accessible, and performant user interfaces.
expertise.backend: Scalable server-side solutions with .NET, Node.js, and SQL databases. Experience with RESTful APIs, microservices, and data processing.
expertise.cloud: Cloud infrastructure on AWS and Azure. Proficient in Docker, CI/CD pipelines, and DevOps practices for high-availability systems.
